headline: Clinical metagenomics: finding pathogens in difficult samples
description: How clinical metagenomics supports difficult diagnoses, from host DNA and noisy databases to clinical interpretation and genomic training.
summary: Hosts Lee Katz and Andrew Page join guests Torsten Seemann and Finlay Maguire to discuss clinical metagenomics when routine microbiology has not explained an infection. They examine sample selection, human DNA, taxonomic profiling and misleading database matches. The conversation presents sequencing as a complementary source of evidence that requires close discussion between bioinformaticians and clinicians.

people.name: Andrew Page
people.affiliation: CTO at Origin Sciences and visiting professor at the University of East Anglia

sections.heading: When routine microbiology leaves questions
sections.body:
Finlay describes clinical metagenomics as an approach used after conventional microbiology workflows, including culture and biochemical tests, have failed to explain a patient's infection. The next step is to sequence the sample deeply and look for evidence that can guide further investigation.

Sample choice depends on the clinical presentation. Blood, blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid and skin swabs are discussed; swabs from sores can contain greater microbial diversity. These difficult hospital cases often involve immunocompromised patients or people with long-term frailty. There may be several concurrent infections rather than one obvious causative organism, and viral pathogens add another challenge to the analysis.

sections.heading: Deep sequencing and multiple profiling tools
sections.body:
Human DNA can dominate the data. Finlay describes sequencing deeply, sometimes using cultures or swabs with less human material, and applying computational host removal. He analyses both the complete dataset and the host-removed dataset to check that filtering has not discarded potentially important microbial reads through sequence similarity to the human genome.

Taxonomic profiling is generally more practical than recovering a good microbial genome from sparse short-read data. Kraken2 and Bracken are discussed, although Finlay's immediate priority is identifying candidates rather than estimating abundance. The taxprofiler workflow is mentioned for bringing several profiling tools together. Marker-gene approaches provide another comparison: they can offer greater specificity, but sensitivity suffers when the required markers are not represented in the reads.

sections.heading: Reference databases can create false leads
sections.body:
Large databases increase the chance of finding an unusual organism, but also introduce noise. Finlay describes using NR alongside other databases and looking for signals that agree across analyses. More curated marker-gene databases can provide a useful cross-check, while unusual bacteria, fungi and parasites may remain poorly represented.

The panel discusses contamination in reference assemblies, including examples involving RefSeq and malaria-related false positives. Human sequence in a falciparum assembly can make human reads appear to support a pathogen identification. More diverse human references also help, because a single human reference does not capture human diversity, and that causes classification problems when samples come from a broader range of populations. Aggressive host filtering, however, creates its own risk of losing useful reads. Database matches therefore need scrutiny rather than automatic acceptance.

sections.heading: Interpretation is an ongoing clinical discussion
sections.body:
Finlay describes the analysis as hypothesis generation followed by repeated conversations with clinical microbiologists. Symptoms, exposure history and published case reports help determine which findings deserve attention. A candidate can prompt a more focused analysis using a customised database and additional reference genomes. Specialist government laboratories may also have relevant expertise or culture capabilities unavailable in a routine clinical laboratory.

In the service he describes, results are generally communicated through discussion rather than a formal report. The shared hospital laboratory is jointly funded by participating hospitals. A panellist distinguishes these discussions from official reports, which bring accreditation and legal responsibilities. Finlay says much of this work happens under research use: it may inform care without being an accredited component of the clinical treatment plan.

sections.heading: Treatment continues while the investigation proceeds
sections.body:
The panel stresses that patients are already being treated while difficult infections are investigated. An early clinical metagenomics example involving Leptospira illustrates this: penicillin was among the treatments being given, and the organism was susceptible. Sequencing was not a reason to leave the patient untreated.

Finlay also recalls a conference talk about a service offering clinical metagenomic testing. There were occasions when unexpected findings improved outcomes, but broad testing could also produce the pathogen equivalent of incidentalomas. As with incidental findings on body scans, detecting something does not establish that it is harmful. Acting on findings that would otherwise cause no problem can itself lead to harm.

sections.heading: Genomic literacy needs formal training
sections.body:
Useful interpretation requires clinicians who understand enough genomics and bioinformaticians who engage with microbiology. Finlay says genomics is not yet part of the core residency competencies for microbiologists in Canada, despite substantial expertise among colleagues. He contrasts this with examination questions that had required interpretation of pulsed-field results and describes efforts to introduce formal Royal College competencies.

Training changes also take time: a potentially five-year programme means new requirements would not immediately produce a fully trained workforce. Public health provides a contrasting example, with PulseNet certification requiring relevant analysis and interpretation. The panel distinguishes having experienced individuals from guaranteeing that everyone entering a role has received genomic training.

quotes.speaker: Finlay Maguire

faq.q: When is clinical metagenomics used in the workflow described?
faq.a: It is used when routine microbiology has not explained an infection. The panel presents it as a complementary investigation while clinicians continue treating the patient.

faq.q: How does human DNA affect clinical metagenomic analysis?
faq.a: Human DNA can dominate the sequencing data. Finlay compares analyses before and after computational host removal because filtering can also remove potentially useful microbial reads.

faq.q: Why can a metagenomic analysis report pathogens that are not causing disease?
faq.a: Reference contamination can produce misleading matches, and detected organisms may be commensals rather than causes of illness. The episode emphasises checking database evidence against symptoms, exposures and clinical expertise.

faq.q: Does every clinical metagenomic analysis produce a formal diagnostic report?
faq.a: Not in the service Finlay describes: results usually support repeated discussions and focused follow-up analyses. The panel distinguishes research-use findings from accredited clinical reports with legal responsibilities.
